extra.message: The 'search' parameter from request.args.get('search') is interpolated directly into a SQLAlchemy text() clause: text(f"text like '%{search_param}%'"). An attacker can break out of the string literal and inject arbitrary SQL (e.g., ' OR 1=1 --) to read or modify notes belonging to other users.

The registration code from form.registration_code.data is concatenated directly into a raw SQL statement executed via session.execute(text(f"... WHERE code = '{code}'")). An attacker can submit a crafted registration_code value to inject SQL, bypass registration code validation, or read arbitrary data from the database.

The 404 error handler interpolates request.path directly into an f-string that is passed to render_template_string: render_template_string(f"{error}. Requested URL was {request.path}"). Because request.path is attacker-controlled and rendered as a Jinja2 template, a request to a URL containing Jinja syntax (e.g. /{{config}} or /{{ ''.__class__.__mro__[1].__subclasses__() }}) results in Server-Side Template Injection, leading to remote code execution and disclosure of secrets such as the Flask SECRET_KEY.

cwe: CWE-94: Improper Control of Generation of Code (Code Injection)

extra.message: The 'preferences' cookie value is base64-decoded and then deserialized with pickle.loads (loads(b64decode(preferences))) inside the before_request hook, which runs for every request. Because the cookie is fully attacker-controlled, a malicious pickle payload can be crafted to execute arbitrary code on the server during deserialization, resulting in unauthenticated remote code execution.

download() calls urllib.request.urlopen(url) with a URL supplied by the user via the /account/image endpoint (form.url.data). The ImageForm URLField performs no scheme/host validation, so an attacker can supply URLs targeting internal services (e.g. http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/) or local files (file:///etc/passwd). The fetched response is base64-encoded and stored as the profile image, allowing the attacker to exfiltrate internal responses / local file contents by viewing their profile.

delete_note() looks up a Note by note_id (session.get(Note, note_id)) and deletes it without verifying that note.user_id matches current_user.id (or that current_user.is_admin). Any authenticated user can delete any other user's note by POSTing to /notes/<arbitrary_note_id>/delete. The ownership check present in the home.html template is not enforced server-side.

cwe: CWE-639: Authorization Bypass Through User-Controlled Key

extra.message: get_personal_notes(user_id) returns all notes where Note.user_id == user_id, including private notes, with no check that user_id equals current_user.id. Any authenticated user can read another user's private notes by requesting /accounts/<other_user_id>/notes, bypassing the privacy flag on notes.

cwe: CWE-639: Authorization Bypass Through User-Controlled Key

extra.message: update_account() copies all submitted form fields (except 'password') directly into current_user.__dict__ via current_user.__dict__.update(filtered_values). AccountForm includes an 'is_admin' BooleanField, so a non-admin user can submit is_admin=on in a crafted POST to /account and escalate privileges to administrator, gaining access to the /registration-codes admin page and admin note-deletion capabilities.

cwe: CWE-915: Improperly Controlled Modification of Dynamically-Determined Object Attributes

extra.message: The POST /account (update_account) route is missing the @login_required decorator, unlike the GET /account route which has it. This allows unauthenticated users to submit state-changing account-update requests. While exploitation is limited because current_user is anonymous without login, the missing authentication on a critical state-changing endpoint is a genuine access-control defect.

cwe: CWE-306: Missing Authentication for Critical Function

extra.message: Note text is rendered with the Jinja2 'safe' filter: {{ note.text | safe }}. Note text is user-controlled (submitted via the CKEditor form on /notes) and is not sanitized, so any user can store an arbitrary JavaScript payload that executes in every viewer's browser when the home page lists the note.

extra.message: render_table is called with safe_columns=['text'], which marks the note 'text' column as safe and disables HTML escaping. Because note text is user-controlled and unsanitized, an attacker can inject arbitrary HTML/JavaScript that executes when search results are rendered.

extra.message: The Flask secret key is hardcoded as app.secret_key = "super secret key". This key signs and encrypts session cookies; anyone who knows it can forge session cookies, impersonate any user (including admins), and tamper with flask-login sessions. It is committed to source control and is a well-known default-style value.

cwe: CWE-321: Use of Hard-coded Cryptographic Key

extra.message: The database is seeded with default users whose passwords are derived from well-known plaintext values: user@evfa.com with password 'user' and admin@evfa.com with password 'admin' (the latter having is_admin=True). These trivial default credentials allow an attacker to authenticate, and the admin account grants full administrative access.

A static registration code 'a36e990b-0024-4d55-b74a-f8d7528e1764' is hardcoded and seeded into the database. Anyone who reads the source can use this code to self-register a new account (including via the SQL-injection-vulnerable signup endpoint), bypassing the intended registration-code access control.

The SQLAlchemy engine is created with echo=True, which logs every SQL statement (including query parameters such as email addresses, note contents, and search terms) to the application logs. In production this can expose sensitive user data and aids an attacker in observing/injecting SQL. Combined with the SQL injection vulnerabilities, echoed logs further leak query structure and results context.

cwe: CWE-532: Insertion of Sensitive Information into Log File
